figures.caption: Figure 1: Geometric overview of CAST. Left: an unseen class’s CLIP text embedding zu (e.g. Penguin) decomposes into an in-span component and an out-of-span residual (Eq. (20)). Middle: the Ridge estimator P̂ (Eq. (12)) is the closed-form coordinate change between the two spaces. Right: seen-class weights obey a predictable structure; the synthesized ŵu differs from the true, unobserved w∗ u by the intrinsic gap and the extrapolation penalty (Proposition 1).

Figure 2: Empirical validation of A1 and A2 on AWA2. (a) Cosine alignment cos(wc, µc) across five architectures (NC3): architectures satisfying NC3 by design concentrate near cos = 1. (b) Unseen accuracy vs. CLIP validation loss during training, rising monotonically as ε → 0 (A2).

Figure 5: Effect of unseen-class description on ρu and synthesis quality, on AWA2. (a) Accuracy vs. bridge quality across description templates (listed in the supplementary material). (b) Per-class accuracy vs. ρu.

Table 1: Zero-shot classification performance on unseen classes using our proposed CAST method, in the conventional zero-shot setting. Red and blue values indicates best and second best performance of classifier per CLIP model. Parenthetical values report top-1 accuracy for synthesized seen-class weights, reflecting bridge reconstruction quality.

Table 2: Generalized zero-shot learning results. The compared methods are image-free only, i.e. they are trained through gradient descent. Our model is the only training-free approach. CLIP linear prope is shown for reference. Best and second-best results per dataset are shown in red and blue, respectively.
Figure 6: Imprinting oracle experiment on AWA2. (a) Accuracy vs. k for k-shot imprinting against CAST and the oracle (k = ∞). (b) Per-class breakdown, tracking ρu (Section 5.2).

Table 3: Zero-shot classification performance on unseen CUB classes, in the same format as Table 1. The consistently lower absolute accuracy relative to AWA2 reflects CUB’s higher semantic extrapolation difficulty ρ̄ (Section 5.2), not a failure specific to any classifier or CLIP backbone.
Table 4: Textual description variants evaluated for encoding unseen classes via CLIP. Each variant represents a different design choice for how semantic information is presented.
